{"type":"reasoning","text":"The user wants me to research and create an impressive HTML simulation of the Operation Black Buck refuelling operation during the Falklands War — the famous Vulcan bomber raids supported by Victor tankers in a complex relay refuelling chain.

Let me first research the facts about Operation Black Buck to get the details right:

**Operation Black Buck background:**
- 1982 Falklands War
- RAF Avro Vulcan bombers flew from Ascension Island to the Falkland Islands (Stanley airfield)
- Round trip was about 6,600-7,600 nautical miles (~12,200 km) — the longest bombing mission in history at that time
- Required a massive refuelling effort with Handley Page Victor K.2 tankers
- Black Buck 1: April 30 - May 1, 1982, flown by Flt Lt Martin Withers (XM607)
- The refuelling plan: 11 Victor tankers + 2 Vulcans (primary + reserve) took off from Ascension
- The famous "tanker cascade" / "tanker pyramid": tankers refuelled other tankers
- Sequence:
  - 11 Victors and 2 Vulcans (XM607 primary, XM598 reserve) took off
  - XM598 (reserve) had a cabin pressurization failure and returned early
  - At various points, tankers topped off other tankers and peeled away
  - Final Victor-to-Vulcan refuelling about 300-400 nm from the Falklands
  - The last Victor (XL189, flown by Bob Tuxford? Actually the last Victor was flown by Sqn Ldr Bob Tuxford) gave more fuel than planned and then had to be refuelled by another Victor on its way back — a "get-well" refuelling
  - Vulcan attacked Stanley airfield runway with 21 × 1,000 lb bombs (only one hit the runway)
  - Return trip refuelling as well

Let me recall the refuelling profile in detail (Black Buck 1):
- Takeoff from Wideawake Airfield, Ascension Island around 23:50-00:20 (April 30, 1982)
- 11 Victor tankers and 2 Vulcans launched (some sources say 11 Victors, 2 Vulcans; plus 2 spare Victors that returned after takeoff checks)
- Refuelling points staged down the route:
  - Refuelling 1: ~85 min after takeoff
  - Multiple top-offs as the formation descended south
  - Tankers peeled away progressively
  - Final refuelling before target: the last Victor gave the Vulcan fuel about 300-400 nm northeast of Stanley; the Victor had to burn/donate more than planned, leaving itself short, requiring a rendezvous with another Victor tanker on the way home ("get well" refuelling near Ascension? Actually it met a tanker launched later)
- Vulcan descended to low level (300 ft) to avoid radar, climbed to 10,000 ft for the attack
- Bomb run at ~03:45-04:00 local time, dropped 21 bombs diagonally across the runway, one direct hit on the runway
- Return: refuelling near Ascension? Actually refuelling about an hour and a half after leaving target? The Vulcan refuelled from a Victor on the return leg
- Total flight time: ~15 hours 45 minutes for the Vulcan
- Distance: ~6,600 nm round trip (~7,600 nm with profile?)

Key numbers I should present (scaled, readable):
- Ascension Island: 7°57′S 14°22′W
- Port Stanley: 51°42′S 57°51′W
- Great-circle distance: ~3,300 nm one way (~6,100 km)
- Round trip: ~6,600-7,600 nm
- 11 Victor K.2 tankers, 2 Vulcans launched; 1 Vulcan + ~7 Victors continued after first refuelling? 

Let me detail the cascade (from Rowland White's "Vulcan 607" and other sources):

Black Buck 1 refuelling plan (the famous cascade):
- 13 aircraft took off at one-minute intervals: 11 Victors + 2 Vulcans (plus 2 reserve Victors that returned once the main force was airborne OK — some sources)
- Seven refuelling brackets southbound:
  1. First refuelling: all 11 Victors top off 2 Vulcans? No...
  
Actually the plan: The Victors were arranged in waves. Pairs of Victors refuelled each other... Let me recall the actual cascade diagram:

The famous diagram shows:
- 11 Victors + 2 Vulcans depart Ascension
- Refuelling point 1 (~600 nm south): Victors transfer fuel to Vulcans and to each other; 2 Victors turn back
- After each bracket, some tankers turn back
- By the last refuelling point (~1,100 nm north of Stanley? No — ~300-400 nm from target), only 1 Victor (XL189, Bob Tuxford) remains with the Vulcan (XM607, Martin Withers)
- The last Victor gives the Vulcan fuel AND stays airborne itself — but due to the Vulcan's higher-than-planned fuel consumption and the tanker giving more than planned, the Victor didn't have enough to get home, so a "reverse" refuelling was arranged with another Victor launched from Ascension to meet it
- 18 tanker sorties total in support of Black Buck 1 (11 outbound + reserves + recovery tankers)

Specific numbers from Vulcan 607 / Wikipedia:
- 11 Victors took off initially along with 2 Vulcans
- The Vulcan reserve (XM598, John Reeve) turned back due to a rubber seal/pressurization failure (direct-vision window seal)
- 7 refuelling points southbound
- At the final refuelling, the Vulcan was about 1,100 nm from Ascension? Hmm, let me think. The final Victor-Vulcan refuelling happened at around 300-400 nm from the target... Actually I recall it being about 1 hour 45 minutes before the target? No...

Let me reconstruct from known facts:
- Total distance Ascension→Stanley: ~3,300 nm
- Cruise speed ~ Mach 0.84 / ~450-480 knots
- Flight time to target ~7.5-8 hours
- Final top-off: The Vulcan needed enough fuel for the low-level run-in (~300 nm at low level), attack, climb, and the long cruise back north to the return refuelling point
- The last refuelling took place around 400 nm northeast of Stanley? I believe the final top-up was around 1,100 nm from Ascension... hmm, that doesn't work: 3,300 - 1,100 = 2,200 nm remaining. Hmm.

From Wikipedia (Operation Black Buck): "The last refuelling was carried out about 300 nautical miles (560 km) from the target" — I think that's right. And the Victor then had to be refuelled by another Victor.

Actually, from Wikipedia: "At around 300 nmi (560 km) from the target, the last Victor turned for home, having transferred more fuel than planned, and had to be refuelled by another Victor on the way back." Yes, I'm fairly confident about the 300 nm figure.

And: "Eleven Victors and two Vulcans took off from Wideawake... The Vulcans were the last to take off... XM598 developed a pressurisation fault and turned back after 30 minutes..." something like that.

I think one refuelling on the way back for the Vulcan, plus the famous one where the last outbound Victor (Tuxford's XL189) got fuel from a Victor flown by... the "get well" tanker. 

18 Victors total flew sorties for Black Buck 1: 11 in the main force (including reserves?), 2 reserve launches, and the rest recovery/relay tankers on the return. Commonly cited: "The mission required 11 Victors for the outbound Vulcan... in total 18 Victor sorties."

**Operations Black Buck 1** to **Black Buck 7** were seven extremely long-range airstrikes conducted during the 1982 [Falklands War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War") by [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") (RAF) [Vulcan bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Vulcan "Avro Vulcan") of the [RAF Waddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Waddington "RAF Waddington") Wing, comprising aircraft from Nos. [44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF"), [50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._50_Squadron_RAF "No. 50 Squadron RAF") and [101 Squadrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._101_Squadron_RAF "No. 101 Squadron RAF"), against Argentine positions in the [Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falkland_Islands "Falkland Islands"). Five of the missions completed attacks. The objective of the missions was to attack [Port Stanley Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Stanley_Airport "Port Stanley Airport") and its associated defences. The raids, at almost 6,600 [nautical miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_mile "Nautical mile") (7,600 [mi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile "Mile"); 12,200 [km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre")) and 16 hours for the round trip, were the longest-ranged bombing raids in history at that time.

The Operation Black Buck raids were staged from [RAF Ascension Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Ascension_Island "RAF Ascension Island"), close to the Equator. The Vulcan was designed for medium-range missions in Europe and lacked the range to fly to the Falklands without refuelling several times. The RAF's tanker planes were mostly converted [Handley Page Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handley_Page_Victor "Handley Page Victor") bombers with similar range, so they too had to be refuelled in the air. A total of eleven tankers were required for two Vulcans (one primary and one reserve), a daunting [logistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistics "Logistics") effort as all aircraft had to use the same runway.

The Vulcans carried either twenty-one 1,000-pound (450 kg) bombs internally or two or four [Shrike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-45_Shrike "AGM-45 Shrike") anti-radar missiles externally. Of the five Black Buck raids flown to completion, three were against Stanley Airfield's runway and operational facilities, while the other two were anti-radar missions using Shrike missiles against a Westinghouse [AN/TPS-43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AN/TPS-43 "AN/TPS-43") long-range 3D radar in the Port Stanley area. Shrikes hit two of the less valuable and rapidly replaced secondary fire control radars, causing some casualties among the Argentine crews. One Vulcan was almost lost when a breakdown of its refueling system forced it to land in Brazil.

The raids did minimal damage to the runway and damage to radars was quickly repaired. A single crater was produced on the runway, rendering it impossible for the airfield to be used by fast jets. Argentine ground crew repaired the runway within twenty-four hours, to a level of quality suitable for [C-130 Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-130_Hercules "C-130 Hercules") transports. The British were aware that the runway remained in use. It has been suggested that the Black Buck raids were undertaken by the RAF because the British armed forces had been cut in the late 1970s and the RAF may have desired a greater role in the conflict to prevent further cuts.

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

During the early 1980s, British defence planning was focused on the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") confrontation with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). Nonetheless, at six-monthly intervals the Defence chiefs reviewed other possible areas of conflict around the globe, including the [Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falkland_Islands "Falkland Islands"). The consensus was that they were indefensible.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1) The nearest airfield usable for operations was on [Ascension Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_Island "Ascension Island"), a British territory in the South Atlantic not far from the equator with a single 10,000-foot (3,000 m) runway at [Wideawake airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wideawake_airfield "Wideawake airfield") that lay 3,700 nautical miles (4,300 mi; 6,900 km) from the UK and 3,300 nautical miles (3,800 mi; 6,100 km) from the Falklands.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman200562–63-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Without aircraft able to cover the long distance, the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") (RAF) could not envisage carrying out operations in the South Atlantic. Activities in the South Atlantic would be carried out by the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") and the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army"), with the RAF's role restricted to the [Hawker Siddeley Nimrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Siddeley_Nimrod "Hawker Siddeley Nimrod") [maritime patrol aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_patrol_aircraft "Maritime patrol aircraft") and logistic support of the base at Ascension by [Vickers VC10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vickers_VC10 "Vickers VC10") and [Lockheed C-130 Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_C-130_Hercules "Lockheed C-130 Hercules") transport aircraft.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–275-4)

Argentine codes had been broken, and in March 1982 intelligence warnings about possible Argentine activity in the South Atlantic accumulated.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELebow200768–70-6) The RAF began examining whether it was possible to carry out long-range operations with [Avro Vulcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Vulcan "Avro Vulcan") [bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber "Bomber") using [aerial refuelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_refuelling "Aerial refuelling").[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–275-4) In 1961, a Vulcan had flown non-stop from the UK to [RAAF Base Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAAF_Base_Richmond "RAAF Base Richmond") near [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") in Australia, a much greater distance,[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) but that was with pre-positioned aerial tankers along the route, which would not be possible flying from Ascension. All consideration at this point was about how it could be done; no targets were identified in the Falklands or Argentina.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201262–63-8)

After [Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_invasion_of_the_Falkland_Islands "1982 invasion of the Falkland Islands") on 2 April 1982,[\[6\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELebow200768–70-6) the British Government resolved to recapture them.[\[9\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman200515–20-9)

### Victor tankers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Victor tankers")\]

Long-range operations were entirely dependent upon the RAF's fleet of [Handley Page Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handley_Page_Victor "Handley Page Victor") K2 tankers.[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201285–86-10) Originally 34 Victors had been built as bombers; 24 had subsequently been converted to tankers. One had been lost in an accident at [RAF Marham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Marham "RAF Marham") on 28 September 1976, leaving the RAF with a force of just 23. These were the only tankers in British service in April 1982; nine VC10s were in the process of being converted to tankers, but conversion of the first was not completed until 22 June.[\[11\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393-11) Of these, twelve were assigned to [No. 55 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._55_Squadron_RAF "No. 55 Squadron RAF") and eleven to [No. 57 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._57_Squadron_RAF "No. 57 Squadron RAF").[\[11\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393-11)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg/250px-RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg)

Victor XM717 (in [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda") in 1984)

The tanker crews were well-trained for their wartime role, as their peacetime role involved refuelling fighters scrambled in response to incursions into British airspace, usually by bombers from the Soviet Union at a rate of five per week.[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201285–86-10) However, long-range flights over the unfamiliar South Atlantic Ocean necessitated upgrades to the Victors' navigational equipment, notably the installation of the [Delco Carousel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delco_Carousel "Delco Carousel") [inertial navigation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_navigation_system "Inertial navigation system") and the [Omega navigation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_\(navigation_system\) "Omega (navigation system)").[\[12\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012119–121-12) The tankers were themselves capable of being refuelled in flight, which meant that it was possible to set up relays of aircraft.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012150–157-13)

The first five Victors deployed to Ascension on 18 April, followed by four more the following day. Another six deployed by the end of the month, bringing the Victor tanker force to fourteen, since one had returned to Marham on 26 April. Each was refuelled by another Victor before leaving UK airspace. While the Victors deployed to Ascension, their normal refuelling mission in the air was undertaken by [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") [Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_KC-135_Stratotanker "Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker"). The station commander at Marham, [Group Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_Captain "Group Captain") J. S. B. Price, became the senior RAF officer at Ascension. [Wing Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_commander_\(rank\) "Wing commander (rank)") D. W. Maurice-Jones assumed command of the Victor detachment at Ascension until 22 April, when he was relieved by Wing Commander A. W. Bowman, the commander of No. 57 Squadron.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393–394-14)

Initial long-range operations by the RAF involved the use of Victor aircraft for reconnaissance of the region surrounding [South Georgia Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_Island "South Georgia Island") in support of [Operation Paraquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Paraquet "Operation Paraquet"), the recapture of South Georgia. At 0400Z on 20 April, a Victor piloted by Squadron Leader J. G. Elliott, took off from Ascension, accompanied by four supporting tankers to supply fuel for the outbound journey. Another flight of four tankers supplied fuel for the return journey. Two more reconnaissance missions to the South Georgia area were carried out on 22–23 April and on 24–25 April.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393–394-14) These missions demonstrated the capability of the Victor tanker fleet, flying out of Ascension, to support operations in the South Atlantic.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012150–157-13)

### Vulcan bombers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Vulcan bombers")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_%2810024511715%29.jpg/250px-Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_%2810024511715%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_\(10024511715\).jpg)

The bomb bay of Vulcan XM598

The Vulcan was the last of the British [V bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_bomber "V bomber") in operational use for bombing, but by March 1982 there were only three squadrons remaining, Nos. [44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF"), [50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._50_Squadron_RAF "No. 50 Squadron RAF") and [101 Squadrons RAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._101_Squadron_RAF "No. 101 Squadron RAF"). All three were scheduled to be disbanded by 1 July 1982.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) They were based at [RAF Waddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Waddington "RAF Waddington") in the UK and assigned to [North Atlantic Treaty Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty_Organization "North Atlantic Treaty Organization") (NATO) for nuclear operations; neither aerial refuelling nor conventional bombing had been practised for several years.[\[16\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201289–90,_123–126-16) A request from [Rear Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_Admiral_\(Royal_Navy\) "Rear Admiral (Royal Navy)") [Sandy Woodward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Woodward "Sandy Woodward"), the commander of the British [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier") group heading south, on 11 April for recommendations for targets to attack in the Falkland Islands led to reconsideration of the possibility of attacks using Vulcans. Options for attacks on airfields and ports on the Argentine mainland were discarded as politically provocative and unlikely to produce worthwhile results. The [Chief of the Air Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_the_Air_Staff_\(United_Kingdom\) "Chief of the Air Staff (United Kingdom)"), [Air Chief Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Chief_Marshal "Air Chief Marshal") Sir [Michael Beetham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Beetham "Michael Beetham") argued that the Vulcan threat would cause the Argentines to retain fighters in the north of Argentina.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005275-17)

Thinking coalesced on a raid on [Port Stanley Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Stanley_Airport "Port Stanley Airport"). Whether it would be worth the effort was debated. Beetham initially proposed an attack in which a single Vulcan would drop seven 1,000-pound (450 kg) bombs. This light bomb load would keep the refuelling requirements down to a minimum. However, tests conducted at the [Garvie Island bombing range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Wrath#Military_use "Cape Wrath") indicated that seven bombs would not be enough, but a full load of twenty-one would have a 90 per cent probability of putting one crater in the runway, with a 75 per cent chance of two craters. An attack was also expected to do damage to the dispersal areas and aircraft parked nearby. To minimise the danger from [anti-aircraft guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-aircraft_gun "Anti-aircraft gun") and [surface-to-air missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile"), the raids would be carried out at night, preferably in bad weather. Damage to the surrounding area, possibly including parked aircraft, would make the raid worthwhile. While the [Chiefs of Staff Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiefs_of_Staff_Committee "Chiefs of Staff Committee") were convinced that the operation was feasible and stood a good chance of success, the civilians at the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_\(United_Kingdom\) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)") were not so certain, and there were political implications to using the base at Ascension for offensive purposes, as Wideawake was technically a USAF base. The [United States Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") was consulted, and affirmed that it had no objection. Authority to proceed with the operation, codenamed Black Buck, was given by the [War Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Cabinet "War Cabinet") on 27 April.[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005275–277-18)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG/250px-XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG)

Vulcan XM607, which carried out the first Black Buck raid

The most controversial part of the plan was the involvement of [Sea Harriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Harriers "Sea Harriers") from Woodward's task force. One of the reasons for the use of the Vulcans was to conserve Sea Harrier resources for the air defence of the naval forces, but the plan required them to conduct a daylight photo reconnaissance sortie over the airfield for the purpose of damage assessment. If they had to be risked, then there were political advantages in using them to carry out the attack on the airport instead. Rear Admiral [Derek Reffell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Reffell "Derek Reffell") proposed that Harriers be used to suppress the airfield radars prior to the Vulcan attack in addition to conducting the post-attack photo reconnaissance. On 29 April, Woodward was informed that the Black Buck raid would occur at 0700Z, and that he was to arrange for the photo reconnaissance to take place as soon as possible afterwards. Woodward signalled that if the photo reconnaissance was essential to Black Buck, then his recommendation was that Black Buck should be cancelled. The following day he was informed that Black Buck had been approved, and that the photo reconnaissance was required not just for damage assessment, but to refute Argentine allegations of indiscriminate bombing.[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005278–279-19)

Vulcans were selected based upon their engines; only those with the more powerful [Bristol Olympus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Olympus "Bristol Olympus") 301 engines were considered suitable.[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201274-20) Six aircraft were selected: two each from Nos. 44, 50 and 101 Squadrons. In the event, one was not used. Five crews were chosen, one each from Nos. 44 and 101 Squadrons, two from No. 50 Squadron, and one from the recently disbanded [No. 9 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._9_Squadron_RAF "No. 9 Squadron RAF").[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) An air-to-air instructor from the [operational conversion unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_conversion_unit "Operational conversion unit") responsible for training personnel to operate Victor tankers was added to each Vulcan crew during operational missions; this officer was responsible for supervising the refuelling contacts.[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrookes200969-21)

One of the most challenging tasks was reinstating the aerial refuelling system, which had been blocked off. This involved replacing the 4-inch (100 mm) [non-return valves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-return_valve "Non-return valve"). Twenty replacements were located on a shelf at [RAF Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Stafford "RAF Stafford").[\[22\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201274–75-22) The five aircraft were fitted with the Carousel inertial navigation system. [AN/ALQ-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AN/ALQ-101 "AN/ALQ-101") [electronic countermeasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_countermeasure "Electronic countermeasure") pods from [Blackburn Buccaneer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackburn_Buccaneer "Blackburn Buccaneer") aircraft at [RAF Honington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Honington "RAF Honington") were fitted to the wings of the Vulcans on improvised pylons, using the attachment points originally intended for the [Skybolt missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skybolt_missile "Skybolt missile").[\[23\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012148–149-23) The undersides of the aircraft were painted Dark Sea Grey.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG/250px-Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG)

[Bristol Olympus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Olympus "Bristol Olympus") 301 jet engine serial number 650179 in the [Aviation Museum of Central Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_Museum_of_Central_Finland "Aviation Museum of Central Finland"). This was the number four (right outermost) engine of Vulcan XM612

While the Vulcans were capable of carrying conventional munitions, this had not been done for a long time. To carry twenty-one bombs, the Vulcan required three sets of bomb carriers, each of which held seven bombs. Their release was controlled by a panel at the navigator's station, known as a *90-way*, that monitored the electrical connections to each bomb, and was said to provide 90 different sequences for releasing the 1,000-pound bombs. None of the Vulcans at Waddington were fitted with the bomb racks or the 90-way. A search of the supply dumps at Waddington and [RAF Scampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Scampton "RAF Scampton") located the 90-way panels, which were fitted and tested, but finding enough septuple bomb carriers proved harder, and at least nine were required. Someone remembered that some had been sold to a scrapyard in [Newark-on-Trent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark-on-Trent "Newark-on-Trent"), and they were retrieved from there. Locating sufficient bombs also proved difficult, and only 167 could be located. Some had cast bomb cases rather than machined ones, which was problematic as they tended to shatter, and this mission required bombs that would penetrate into the ground.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012126–127-24) Training of crews in conventional bombing and in-flight refuelling was carried out from 14 to 17 April, when Military Air Traffic Controllers from the Military Area Service (M.A.S.) suite at [London Terminal Control Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Terminal_Control_Centre "London Terminal Control Centre") in West Drayton, Middlesex, took the Vulcan bombers and Victor tankers 250 miles off [Land's End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land's_End "Land's End") in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"), where the vast majority of their aerial refuelling training was completed, always at night.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)

The first two Vulcans, commanded by Squadron Leader John Reeve, and [Flight Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_Lieutenant "Flight Lieutenant") [Martin Withers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Withers?action=edit&redlink=1 "Martin Withers (page does not exist)"), left Waddington at 0900Z on 29 April and arrived at Wideawake at 1800Z after a non-stop nine-hour flight during which they were twice refuelled by Victor tankers.[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012237–240-25)[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) Two other Vulcans subsequently deployed to Wideawake: one commanded by Squadron Leader Alastair Montgomery arrived on 14 May, and another, commanded by Squadron Leader Neil McDougall, on 27 May. It carried out trials with the [Martel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martel_\(missile\) "Martel (missile)") anti-radar missile before being equipped with the [Shrike missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-45_Shrike "AGM-45 Shrike").[\[26\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012365–366-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986365-27)

### Black Buck One

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Black Buck One")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/RAF_Museum%2C_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg/250px-RAF_Museum%2C_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAF_Museum,_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg)

XM598 at [Royal Air Force Museum Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force_Museum_Midlands "Royal Air Force Museum Midlands")

The first surprise attack on the islands, on 30 April – 1 May, was the first significant offensive action made by British forces against the Argentine forces in the Falklands.[\[29\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–277-29) It was aimed at the main runway at Port Stanley Airport. Carrying twenty-one 1,000-pound bombs, the bomber was to fly across the line of the runway at about 35 degrees. The bomb release system was timed to drop bombs sequentially from 10,000 feet (3,000 m), so that at least one bomb would hit the runway.[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012252–253-30) The Vulcan's [fuel tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_tank "Fuel tank") could contain 9,200 imperial gallons (42,000 L) weighing 74,000 pounds (34,000 kg) in fourteen pressurised bag tanks, five in each wing and four in the fuselage. Based upon estimates of the Vulcan's fuel need, eleven Victor tankers, including two reserve aircraft, were assigned to refuel the single Vulcan before and after its attack on the Falklands.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986394-31) Two Vulcans were assigned to the mission: one, commanded by Reeve, was the lead with another, captained by Withers, as the reserve, which would return to Ascension once Reeve had successfully completed its first aerial refuelling.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) The plan called for 15 Victor sorties and 18 aerial refuellings.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986394-31) At the time it was the longest bombing mission ever attempted.[\[32\]](#cite_note-RAF-32) ([B-2 Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-2_Spirit "B-2 Spirit") bombers would surpass that record during the 2001 [Operation Enduring Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Enduring_Freedom "Operation Enduring Freedom").)[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

The eleven Victors and two Vulcans began taking off from Wideawake at 2350Z at one-minute intervals, with Reeve's Vulcan the eleventh to lift off and Withers's the last.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012266–267-34) With a full load of bombs and fuel, a sixth crew member and a fresh coat of paint, the Vulcans were well over their rated maximum takeoff weight of 204,000 pounds (93,000 kg). On the warm Ascension Island, the Bristol Olympus 301 engines had to be run at 103 per cent of their rated power in order to get the Vulcans airborne.[\[32\]](#cite_note-RAF-32) Shortly after takeoff, Reeve suffered a failure. A rubber seal on the captain's "direct vision" side window had perished. Unable to close or seal the window and pressurise the crew cabin, he was forced to return to Ascension. The Vulcan lacked the ability to dump fuel, and it was far too heavy even for an emergency landing, so the crew were forced to remain airborne in a cold and noisy cabin until sufficient fuel had been consumed. Withers took over as the primary Vulcan. Twenty minutes later, one of the Victor tankers returned to Ascension with a faulty refuelling hose system, and its place was taken by the reserve.[\[35\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012267–270-35)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Refuelling.plan.black.buck.svg/250px-Refuelling.plan.black.buck.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Refuelling.plan.black.buck.svg)

The attacking Vulcan was refuelled seven times on the outward journey and once on the return journey. Grey lines indicate reserve aircraft to replace casualties.

In the 34 minutes between the first and second refuellings, Withers's Vulcan burned through 9,200 pounds (4,200 kg) of fuel, at the rate of 16,250 pounds (7,370 kg) per hour. All this time its weight never dropped below the theoretical maximum.[\[36\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012280-36) At the end of the second refuelling, two more tankers peeled off and returned, reducing the force to just three: Withers's Vulcan, a Victor flown by Squadron Leader Bob Tuxford, and a Victor flown by Flight Lieutenant Steve Biglands.[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012285-37) As a result of the fuel demand and problems in flight with refuelling, two of the Victors had to fly further south than planned, reducing their own reserves. At the final refuelling bracket, the sortie flew into a violent thunderstorm, during which Biglands's refuelling probe failed.[\[38\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012291–296-38)

Tuxford was supposed to return after this refuelling with 64,000 pounds (29,000 kg) of fuel while Biglands flew on with the Vulcan, but Tuxford now took Biglands's place. A quick calculation showed that he did not have enough fuel to make it back to Ascension.[\[39\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012300–302-39) It fell to Tuxford to conduct the final refuelling. Withers received 7,000 pounds (3,200 kg) less than he expected. This meant that he would be making the return fuelling rendezvous with 7,000 pounds (3,200 kg) in his tanks instead of 14,000 pounds (6,400 kg).[\[40\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012306–311-40)

Now alone, Withers flew on to the Falklands. He made his approach at low level, dropping to 300 feet (91 m) before climbing to 1,000 feet (300 m) for the bomb run 40 miles (64 km) from the target.[\[32\]](#cite_note-RAF-32) To verify their position and minimise the risk of civilian casualties, the [H2S radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H2S_radar "H2S radar") was successfully locked on to the 2,313-foot (705 m) peak of [Mount Usborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Usborne "Mount Usborne"), 33 miles (53 km) west of Stanley, before the automated bombing control system was engaged.[\[41\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012318–320-41) Withers made the final approach at 10,000 feet (3,000 m), with an airspeed of 330 knots (610 km/h). The Vulcan's electronic countermeasures defeated the radar systems controlling the defending [Skyguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oerlikon_35_mm_twin_cannon "Oerlikon 35 mm twin cannon") anti-aircraft cannons. The twenty-one bombs were dropped. Once all were away, Withers put the Vulcan into a 60-degree bank to the left, subjecting the crew to 2 *g* (20 m/s2), twice the force of gravity.[\[42\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012324–328-42) Sea Harriers of [801 Naval Air Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/801_Naval_Air_Squadron "801 Naval Air Squadron") (NAS) were held at readiness on board the aircraft carrier [HMS *Invincible*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Invincible_\(R05\) "HMS Invincible (R05)") to protect the Vulcan, but were not required as no Argentine aircraft were in the area at the time of the attack.[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986210-43) The Sea Harriers went into action shortly after the Vulcan raid. Two of the aircraft flew over Port Stanley airport to photograph the damage caused by the Vulcan.[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200978-44)

Withers climbed away from the airfield and headed nearly due north to a planned rendezvous with a Victor some way off the Brazilian coast near [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"). As they passed the British Task Force, the crew signalled the code word "superfuse" indicating a successful attack at 0746Z.[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986365-27) Their journey continued within range of the South American coast to the rendezvous with a Victor flown by Squadron Leader Barry Neal. After contacting control with an update, the tanker was sent further south. To help bring the two planes together, one of Ascension's two Nimrod maritime reconnaissance aircraft flew from Wideawake to the area. Without an in-flight refuelling system, it was unable to remain for long.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012338–341-45) Tuxford, who had continued to maintain radio silence lest he compromise the mission, picked up the "superfuse" signal and radioed Ascension for help.[\[46\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986395-46) A Victor flown by his squadron commander, Wing Commander Colin Seymour, flew out to meet him, and refuelled Tuxford's Victor, enabling him to return to Ascension 14 hours and 5 minutes after he had left. Meanwhile, with the help of the Nimrod, Withers made the rendezvous with Neal, and all three aircraft returned to Ascension safely.[\[47\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012344–348-47) Withers touched down at 1452Z.[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986365-27)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Vulcan_bomber_18_May_1982.JPG/250px-Vulcan_bomber_18_May_1982.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vulcan_bomber_18_May_1982.JPG)

A Vulcan bomber makes an approach to land at Ascension Island at dusk

[Northwood Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwood_Headquarters "Northwood Headquarters") received the "superfuse" message by 0830Z and the Ministry of Defence shortly thereafter. Beetham was informed by his deputy, [Air Vice Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Vice_Marshal "Air Vice Marshal") [Kenneth Hayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Hayr "Kenneth Hayr"), an hour later.[\[48\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012337-48) The news of the bombing raid was reported on the [BBC World Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_World_Service "BBC World Service") before either the Vulcan or the last tanker arrived back at Ascension.[\[49\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012343-49) The bombardment is believed to have killed three Argentine personnel at the airport and injured several more. One bomb exploded on the runway and caused a large crater which proved difficult to repair, and the other bombs caused minor damage to aircraft and equipment. The shortened runway remained in action.[\[50\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200977–78-50)

Later that morning, twelve [800 Naval Air Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_Naval_Air_Squadron "800 Naval Air Squadron") Sea Harriers were dispatched from the aircraft carrier [HMS *Hermes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Hermes_\(R12\) "HMS Hermes (R12)") to attack targets on East Falkland.[\[51\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986193-51) Nine of the aircraft struck Port Stanley Airport and dropped 27 bombs on the airfield and its defences. The bombs set a stockpile of fuel on fire and may have slightly damaged the runway.[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200978-44) One of the Sea Harriers was struck by a 20 mm anti-aircraft round, which damaged its fin and tailplane; the aircraft managed to return to *Hermes* and was quickly repaired.[\[52\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986194-52) The Argentine air defence headquarters incorrectly assessed British losses as three aircraft destroyed.[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200978-44)

The other three 800 NAS Sea Harriers attacked the airfield at [Goose Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goose_Green "Goose Green") with [cluster bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_munition "Cluster munition") shortly after the raid on Port Stanley, resulting in the destruction of a [Pucará](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMA_IA_58_Pucará "FMA IA 58 Pucará") and severe damage to another two. The pilot of the destroyed aircraft and five maintenance personnel were killed. Neither of the two damaged aircraft flew again.[\[53\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200979-53) The three British aircraft did not encounter any opposition and safely returned to *Hermes*.[\[52\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986194-52) After the aircraft were refuelled, 800 NAS began launching Sea Harriers on combat air patrol sorties.[\[52\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986194-52) 801 NAS maintained a four-aircraft combat air patrol to the east of Port Stanley throughout the operation.[\[43\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986210-43)

**Great circle builder:**
```js
function gcPoints(a, b, n){
  // a,b: [lat,lng] degrees
  const toV = ([lat,lng])=>{const la=lat*Math.PI/180, lo=lng*Math.PI/180;
    return [Math.cos(la)*Math.cos(lo), Math.cos(la)*Math.sin(lo), Math.sin(la)];};
  const A=toV(a), B=toV(b);
  const dot=A[0]*B[0]+A[1]*B[1]+A[2]*B[2];
  const ang=Math.acos(Math.min(1,Math.max(-1,dot)));
  const pts=[];
  for(let i=0;i<=n;i++){
    const f=i/n, s=Math.sin((1-f)*ang)/Math.sin(ang), c=Math.sin(f*ang)/Math.sin(ang);
    const v=[A[0]*s+B[0]*c, A[1]*s+B[1]*c, A[2]*s+B[2]*c];
    const lat=Math.atan2(v[2], Math.hypot(v[0],v[1]))*180/Math.PI;
    const lng=Math.atan2(v[1], v[0])*180/Math.PI;
    pts.push([lat,lng]);
  }
  return pts;
}
```

```js
function makeTrack(pts){ // pts: [[lat,lng]...]
  // world coords
  const REF = -29*Math.PI/180, K=Math.cos(REF);
  const w = pts.map(([la,lo])=>[lo*K, -la]); // x,y world (deg-ish)
  const cum=[0];
  for(let i=1;i<w.length;i++){
    const dLa=pts[i][0]-pts[i-1][0], dLo=pts[i][1]-pts[i-1][1];
    const nm = 60*Math.hypot(dLa, dLo*Math.cos((pts[i][0]+pts[i-1][0])/2*Math.PI/180));
    cum.push(cum[i-1]+nm);
  }
  return {pts, w, cum, len:cum[cum.length-1],
    pointAt(d){ /* binary search + lerp in world */ },
    latLngAt(d){...}
  };
}
```

**Operations Black Buck 1** to **Black Buck 7** were seven extremely long-range airstrikes conducted during the 1982 [Falklands War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War") by [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") (RAF) [Vulcan bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Vulcan "Avro Vulcan") of the [RAF Waddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Waddington "RAF Waddington") Wing, comprising aircraft from Nos. [44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF"), [50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._50_Squadron_RAF "No. 50 Squadron RAF") and [101 Squadrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._101_Squadron_RAF "No. 101 Squadron RAF"), against Argentine positions in the [Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falkland_Islands "Falkland Islands"). Five of the missions completed attacks. The objective of the missions was to attack [Port Stanley Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Stanley_Airport "Port Stanley Airport") and its associated defences. The raids, at almost 6,600 [nautical miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_mile "Nautical mile") (7,600 [mi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile "Mile"); 12,200 [km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre")) and 16 hours for the round trip, were the longest-ranged bombing raids in history at that time.

The Operation Black Buck raids were staged from [RAF Ascension Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Ascension_Island "RAF Ascension Island"), close to the Equator. The Vulcan was designed for medium-range missions in Europe and lacked the range to fly to the Falklands without refuelling several times. The RAF's tanker planes were mostly converted [Handley Page Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handley_Page_Victor "Handley Page Victor") bombers with similar range, so they too had to be refuelled in the air. A total of eleven tankers were required for two Vulcans (one primary and one reserve), a daunting [logistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistics "Logistics") effort as all aircraft had to use the same runway.

The Vulcans carried either twenty-one 1,000-pound (450 kg) bombs internally or two or four [Shrike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-45_Shrike "AGM-45 Shrike") anti-radar missiles externally. Of the five Black Buck raids flown to completion, three were against Stanley Airfield's runway and operational facilities, while the other two were anti-radar missions using Shrike missiles against a Westinghouse [AN/TPS-43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AN/TPS-43 "AN/TPS-43") long-range 3D radar in the Port Stanley area. Shrikes hit two of the less valuable and rapidly replaced secondary fire control radars, causing some casualties among the Argentine crews. One Vulcan was almost lost when a breakdown of its refueling system forced it to land in Brazil.

The raids did minimal damage to the runway and damage to radars was quickly repaired. A single crater was produced on the runway, rendering it impossible for the airfield to be used by fast jets. Argentine ground crew repaired the runway within twenty-four hours, to a level of quality suitable for [C-130 Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-130_Hercules "C-130 Hercules") transports. The British were aware that the runway remained in use. It has been suggested that the Black Buck raids were undertaken by the RAF because the British armed forces had been cut in the late 1970s and the RAF may have desired a greater role in the conflict to prevent further cuts.

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

During the early 1980s, British defence planning was focused on the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") confrontation with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). Nonetheless, at six-monthly intervals the Defence chiefs reviewed other possible areas of conflict around the globe, including the [Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falkland_Islands "Falkland Islands"). The consensus was that they were indefensible.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1) The nearest airfield usable for operations was on [Ascension Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_Island "Ascension Island"), a British territory in the South Atlantic not far from the equator with a single 10,000-foot (3,000 m) runway at [Wideawake airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wideawake_airfield "Wideawake airfield") that lay 3,700 nautical miles (4,300 mi; 6,900 km) from the UK and 3,300 nautical miles (3,800 mi; 6,100 km) from the Falklands.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman200562–63-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Without aircraft able to cover the long distance, the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") (RAF) could not envisage carrying out operations in the South Atlantic. Activities in the South Atlantic would be carried out by the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") and the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army"), with the RAF's role restricted to the [Hawker Siddeley Nimrod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Siddeley_Nimrod "Hawker Siddeley Nimrod") [maritime patrol aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_patrol_aircraft "Maritime patrol aircraft") and logistic support of the base at Ascension by [Vickers VC10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vickers_VC10 "Vickers VC10") and [Lockheed C-130 Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_C-130_Hercules "Lockheed C-130 Hercules") transport aircraft.[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–275-4)

Argentine codes had been broken, and in March 1982 intelligence warnings about possible Argentine activity in the South Atlantic accumulated.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELebow200768–70-6) The RAF began examining whether it was possible to carry out long-range operations with [Avro Vulcan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Vulcan "Avro Vulcan") [bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber "Bomber") using [aerial refuelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_refuelling "Aerial refuelling").[\[1\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201235-1)[\[4\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–275-4) In 1961, a Vulcan had flown non-stop from the UK to [RAAF Base Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAAF_Base_Richmond "RAAF Base Richmond") near [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") in Australia, a much greater distance,[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) but that was with pre-positioned aerial tankers along the route, which would not be possible flying from Ascension. All consideration at this point was about how it could be done; no targets were identified in the Falklands or Argentina.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201262–63-8)

After [Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_invasion_of_the_Falkland_Islands "1982 invasion of the Falkland Islands") on 2 April 1982,[\[6\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELebow200768–70-6) the British Government resolved to recapture them.[\[9\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman200515–20-9)

### Victor tankers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Victor tankers")\]

Long-range operations were entirely dependent upon the RAF's fleet of [Handley Page Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handley_Page_Victor "Handley Page Victor") K2 tankers.[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201285–86-10) Originally 34 Victors had been built as bombers; 24 had subsequently been converted to tankers. One had been lost in an accident at [RAF Marham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Marham "RAF Marham") on 28 September 1976, leaving the RAF with a force of just 23. These were the only tankers in British service in April 1982; nine VC10s were in the process of being converted to tankers, but conversion of the first was not completed until 22 June.[\[11\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393-11) Of these, twelve were assigned to [No. 55 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._55_Squadron_RAF "No. 55 Squadron RAF") and eleven to [No. 57 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._57_Squadron_RAF "No. 57 Squadron RAF").[\[11\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393-11)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg/250px-RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAF_Victor_in_Bermuda.jpg)

Victor XM717 (in [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda") in 1984)

The tanker crews were well-trained for their wartime role, as their peacetime role involved refuelling fighters scrambled in response to incursions into British airspace, usually by bombers from the Soviet Union at a rate of five per week.[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201285–86-10) However, long-range flights over the unfamiliar South Atlantic Ocean necessitated upgrades to the Victors' navigational equipment, notably the installation of the [Delco Carousel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delco_Carousel "Delco Carousel") [inertial navigation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inertial_navigation_system "Inertial navigation system") and the [Omega navigation system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_\(navigation_system\) "Omega (navigation system)").[\[12\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012119–121-12) The tankers were themselves capable of being refuelled in flight, which meant that it was possible to set up relays of aircraft.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012150–157-13)

The first five Victors deployed to Ascension on 18 April, followed by four more the following day. Another six deployed by the end of the month, bringing the Victor tanker force to fourteen, since one had returned to Marham on 26 April. Each was refuelled by another Victor before leaving UK airspace. While the Victors deployed to Ascension, their normal refuelling mission in the air was undertaken by [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") [Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_KC-135_Stratotanker "Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker"). The station commander at Marham, [Group Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_Captain "Group Captain") J. S. B. Price, became the senior RAF officer at Ascension. [Wing Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_commander_\(rank\) "Wing commander (rank)") D. W. Maurice-Jones assumed command of the Victor detachment at Ascension until 22 April, when he was relieved by Wing Commander A. W. Bowman, the commander of No. 57 Squadron.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393–394-14)

Initial long-range operations by the RAF involved the use of Victor aircraft for reconnaissance of the region surrounding [South Georgia Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_Island "South Georgia Island") in support of [Operation Paraquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Paraquet "Operation Paraquet"), the recapture of South Georgia. At 0400Z on 20 April, a Victor piloted by Squadron Leader J. G. Elliott, took off from Ascension, accompanied by four supporting tankers to supply fuel for the outbound journey. Another flight of four tankers supplied fuel for the return journey. Two more reconnaissance missions to the South Georgia area were carried out on 22–23 April and on 24–25 April.[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986393–394-14) These missions demonstrated the capability of the Victor tanker fleet, flying out of Ascension, to support operations in the South Atlantic.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012150–157-13)

### Vulcan bombers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Vulcan bombers")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_%2810024511715%29.jpg/250px-Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_%2810024511715%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vulcan_Bomb_Bay_\(10024511715\).jpg)

The bomb bay of Vulcan XM598

The Vulcan was the last of the British [V bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_bomber "V bomber") in operational use for bombing, but by March 1982 there were only three squadrons remaining, Nos. [44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF"), [50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._50_Squadron_RAF "No. 50 Squadron RAF") and [101 Squadrons RAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._101_Squadron_RAF "No. 101 Squadron RAF"). All three were scheduled to be disbanded by 1 July 1982.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) They were based at [RAF Waddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Waddington "RAF Waddington") in the UK and assigned to [North Atlantic Treaty Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty_Organization "North Atlantic Treaty Organization") (NATO) for nuclear operations; neither aerial refuelling nor conventional bombing had been practised for several years.[\[16\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201289–90,_123–126-16) A request from [Rear Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_Admiral_\(Royal_Navy\) "Rear Admiral (Royal Navy)") [Sandy Woodward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Woodward "Sandy Woodward"), the commander of the British [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier") group heading south, on 11 April for recommendations for targets to attack in the Falkland Islands led to reconsideration of the possibility of attacks using Vulcans. Options for attacks on airfields and ports on the Argentine mainland were discarded as politically provocative and unlikely to produce worthwhile results. The [Chief of the Air Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_the_Air_Staff_\(United_Kingdom\) "Chief of the Air Staff (United Kingdom)"), [Air Chief Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Chief_Marshal "Air Chief Marshal") Sir [Michael Beetham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Beetham "Michael Beetham") argued that the Vulcan threat would cause the Argentines to retain fighters in the north of Argentina.[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005275-17)

Thinking coalesced on a raid on [Port Stanley Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Stanley_Airport "Port Stanley Airport"). Whether it would be worth the effort was debated. Beetham initially proposed an attack in which a single Vulcan would drop seven 1,000-pound (450 kg) bombs. This light bomb load would keep the refuelling requirements down to a minimum. However, tests conducted at the [Garvie Island bombing range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Wrath#Military_use "Cape Wrath") indicated that seven bombs would not be enough, but a full load of twenty-one would have a 90 per cent probability of putting one crater in the runway, with a 75 per cent chance of two craters. An attack was also expected to do damage to the dispersal areas and aircraft parked nearby. To minimise the danger from [anti-aircraft guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-aircraft_gun "Anti-aircraft gun") and [surface-to-air missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile"), the raids would be carried out at night, preferably in bad weather. Damage to the surrounding area, possibly including parked aircraft, would make the raid worthwhile. While the [Chiefs of Staff Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiefs_of_Staff_Committee "Chiefs of Staff Committee") were convinced that the operation was feasible and stood a good chance of success, the civilians at the [Ministry of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_\(United_Kingdom\) "Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)") were not so certain, and there were political implications to using the base at Ascension for offensive purposes, as Wideawake was technically a USAF base. The [United States Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") was consulted, and affirmed that it had no objection. Authority to proceed with the operation, codenamed Black Buck, was given by the [War Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Cabinet "War Cabinet") on 27 April.[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005275–277-18)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG/250px-XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:XM607_SIDE_VIEW.JPG)

Vulcan XM607, which carried out the first Black Buck raid

The most controversial part of the plan was the involvement of [Sea Harriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Harriers "Sea Harriers") from Woodward's task force. One of the reasons for the use of the Vulcans was to conserve Sea Harrier resources for the air defence of the naval forces, but the plan required them to conduct a daylight photo reconnaissance sortie over the airfield for the purpose of damage assessment. If they had to be risked, then there were political advantages in using them to carry out the attack on the airport instead. Rear Admiral [Derek Reffell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Reffell "Derek Reffell") proposed that Harriers be used to suppress the airfield radars prior to the Vulcan attack in addition to conducting the post-attack photo reconnaissance. On 29 April, Woodward was informed that the Black Buck raid would occur at 0700Z, and that he was to arrange for the photo reconnaissance to take place as soon as possible afterwards. Woodward signalled that if the photo reconnaissance was essential to Black Buck, then his recommendation was that Black Buck should be cancelled. The following day he was informed that Black Buck had been approved, and that the photo reconnaissance was required not just for damage assessment, but to refute Argentine allegations of indiscriminate bombing.[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005278–279-19)

Vulcans were selected based upon their engines; only those with the more powerful [Bristol Olympus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Olympus "Bristol Olympus") 301 engines were considered suitable.[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201274-20) Six aircraft were selected: two each from Nos. 44, 50 and 101 Squadrons. In the event, one was not used. Five crews were chosen, one each from Nos. 44 and 101 Squadrons, two from No. 50 Squadron, and one from the recently disbanded [No. 9 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._9_Squadron_RAF "No. 9 Squadron RAF").[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) An air-to-air instructor from the [operational conversion unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_conversion_unit "Operational conversion unit") responsible for training personnel to operate Victor tankers was added to each Vulcan crew during operational missions; this officer was responsible for supervising the refuelling contacts.[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrookes200969-21)

One of the most challenging tasks was reinstating the aerial refuelling system, which had been blocked off. This involved replacing the 4-inch (100 mm) [non-return valves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-return_valve "Non-return valve"). Twenty replacements were located on a shelf at [RAF Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Stafford "RAF Stafford").[\[22\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201274–75-22) The five aircraft were fitted with the Carousel inertial navigation system. [AN/ALQ-101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AN/ALQ-101 "AN/ALQ-101") [electronic countermeasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_countermeasure "Electronic countermeasure") pods from [Blackburn Buccaneer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackburn_Buccaneer "Blackburn Buccaneer") aircraft at [RAF Honington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Honington "RAF Honington") were fitted to the wings of the Vulcans on improvised pylons, using the attachment points originally intended for the [Skybolt missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skybolt_missile "Skybolt missile").[\[23\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012148–149-23) The undersides of the aircraft were painted Dark Sea Grey.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG/250px-Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rolls-Royce_Bristol_Siddeley_Olympus_Mk.301_Keski-Suomen_ilmailumuseo_2.JPG)

[Bristol Olympus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Olympus "Bristol Olympus") 301 jet engine serial number 650179 in the [Aviation Museum of Central Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_Museum_of_Central_Finland "Aviation Museum of Central Finland"). This was the number four (right outermost) engine of Vulcan XM612

While the Vulcans were capable of carrying conventional munitions, this had not been done for a long time. To carry twenty-one bombs, the Vulcan required three sets of bomb carriers, each of which held seven bombs. Their release was controlled by a panel at the navigator's station, known as a *90-way*, that monitored the electrical connections to each bomb, and was said to provide 90 different sequences for releasing the 1,000-pound bombs. None of the Vulcans at Waddington were fitted with the bomb racks or the 90-way. A search of the supply dumps at Waddington and [RAF Scampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Scampton "RAF Scampton") located the 90-way panels, which were fitted and tested, but finding enough septuple bomb carriers proved harder, and at least nine were required. Someone remembered that some had been sold to a scrapyard in [Newark-on-Trent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark-on-Trent "Newark-on-Trent"), and they were retrieved from there. Locating sufficient bombs also proved difficult, and only 167 could be located. Some had cast bomb cases rather than machined ones, which was problematic as they tended to shatter, and this mission required bombs that would penetrate into the ground.[\[24\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012126–127-24) Training of crews in conventional bombing and in-flight refuelling was carried out from 14 to 17 April, when Military Air Traffic Controllers from the Military Area Service (M.A.S.) suite at [London Terminal Control Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Terminal_Control_Centre "London Terminal Control Centre") in West Drayton, Middlesex, took the Vulcan bombers and Victor tankers 250 miles off [Land's End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land's_End "Land's End") in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"), where the vast majority of their aerial refuelling training was completed, always at night.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)

The first two Vulcans, commanded by Squadron Leader John Reeve, and [Flight Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_Lieutenant "Flight Lieutenant") [Martin Withers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Withers?action=edit&redlink=1 "Martin Withers (page does not exist)"), left Waddington at 0900Z on 29 April and arrived at Wideawake at 1800Z after a non-stop nine-hour flight during which they were twice refuelled by Victor tankers.[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012237–240-25)[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) Two other Vulcans subsequently deployed to Wideawake: one commanded by Squadron Leader Alastair Montgomery arrived on 14 May, and another, commanded by Squadron Leader Neil McDougall, on 27 May. It carried out trials with the [Martel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martel_\(missile\) "Martel (missile)") anti-radar missile before being equipped with the [Shrike missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-45_Shrike "AGM-45 Shrike").[\[26\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012365–366-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986365-27)

### Black Buck One

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Operation_Black_Buck&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Black Buck One")\]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/RAF_Museum%2C_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg/250px-RAF_Museum%2C_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAF_Museum,_Cosford_-_geograph.org.uk_-_398691.jpg)

XM598 at [Royal Air Force Museum Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force_Museum_Midlands "Royal Air Force Museum Midlands")

The first surprise attack on the islands, on 30 April – 1 May, was the first significant offensive action made by British forces against the Argentine forces in the Falklands.[\[29\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman2005274–277-29) It was aimed at the main runway at Port Stanley Airport. Carrying twenty-one 1,000-pound bombs, the bomber was to fly across the line of the runway at about 35 degrees. The bomb release system was timed to drop bombs sequentially from 10,000 feet (3,000 m), so that at least one bomb would hit the runway.[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012252–253-30) The Vulcan's [fuel tanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_tank "Fuel tank") could contain 9,200 imperial gallons (42,000 L) weighing 74,000 pounds (34,000 kg) in fourteen pressurised bag tanks, five in each wing and four in the fuselage. Based upon estimates of the Vulcan's fuel need, eleven Victor tankers, including two reserve aircraft, were assigned to refuel the single Vulcan before and after its attack on the Falklands.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986394-31) Two Vulcans were assigned to the mission: one, commanded by Reeve, was the lead with another, captained by Withers, as the reserve, which would return to Ascension once Reeve had successfully completed its first aerial refuelling.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15) The plan called for 15 Victor sorties and 18 aerial refuellings.[\[31\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986394-31) At the time it was the longest bombing mission ever attempted.[\[32\]](#cite_note-RAF-32) ([B-2 Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-2_Spirit "B-2 Spirit") bombers would surpass that record during the 2001 [Operation Enduring Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Enduring_Freedom "Operation Enduring Freedom").)[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

The eleven Victors and two Vulcans began taking off from Wideawake at 2350Z at one-minute intervals, with Reeve's Vulcan the eleventh to lift off and Withers's the last.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986363-15)[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012266–267-34) With a full load of bombs and fuel, a sixth crew member and a fresh coat of paint, the Vulcans were well over their rated maximum takeoff weight of 204,000 pounds (93,000 kg). On the warm Ascension Island, the Bristol Olympus 301 engines had to be run at 103 per cent of their rated power in order to get the Vulcans airborne.[\[32\]](#cite_note-RAF-32) Shortly after takeoff, Reeve suffered a failure. A rubber seal on the captain's "direct vision" side window had perished. Unable to close or seal the window and pressurise the crew cabin, he was forced to return to Ascension. The attacking Vulcan was refuelled seven times on the outward journey and once on the return journey. Grey lines indicate reserve aircraft to replace casualties.

In the 34 minutes between the first and second refuellings, Withers's Vulcan burned through 9,200 pounds (4,200 kg) of fuel, at the rate of 16,250 pounds (7,370 kg) per hour. All this time its weight never dropped below the theoretical maximum.[\[36\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012280-36) At the end of the second refuelling, two more tankers peeled off and returned, reducing the force to just three: Withers's Vulcan, a Victor flown by Squadron Leader Bob Tuxford, and a Victor flown by Flight Lieutenant Steve Biglands.[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012285-37) As a result of the fuel demand and problems in flight with refuelling, two of the Victors had to fly further south than planned, reducing their own reserves. Tuxford was supposed to return after this refuelling with 64,000 pounds (29,000 kg) of fuel while Biglands flew on with the Vulcan, but Tuxford now took Biglands's place. Withers received 7,000 pounds (3,200 kg) less than he expected. Now alone, Withers flew on to the Falklands. Two of the aircraft flew over Port Stanley airport to photograph the damage caused by the Vulcan.[\[44\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiddlebrook200978-44)

Withers climbed away from the airfield and headed nearly due north to a planned rendezvous with a Victor some way off the Brazilian coast near [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"). As they passed the British Task Force, the crew signalled the code word "superfuse" indicating a successful attack at 0746Z.[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986365-27) Their journey continued within range of the South American coast to the rendezvous with a Victor flown by Squadron Leader Barry Neal. After contacting control with an update, the tanker was sent further south. To help bring the two planes together, one of Ascension's two Nimrod maritime reconnaissance aircraft flew from Wideawake to the area. Without an in-flight refuelling system, it was unable to remain for long.[\[45\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2012338–341-45) Tuxford, who had continued to maintain radio silence lest he compromise the mission, picked up the "superfuse" signal and radioed Ascension for help.[\[46\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurdenDraperRoughSmith1986395-46) A Victor flown by his squadron commander, Wing Commander Colin Seymour, flew out to meet him, and refuelled Tuxford's Victor, enabling him to return to Ascension 14 hours and 5 minutes after he had left. function toLL(v){const la=Math.asin(v[2]); const lo=Math.atan2(v[1],v[0]); return [la/D2R, lo/D2R];}
```js
function slerpLL(a,b,u){va=toV(a);vb=toV(b);dot=clamp;ang=acos(dot); if ang<1e-6 return a; slerp formula; return toLL}
```

```js
function slerpLL(a,b,u){
  const va=toV(a),vb=toV(b);
  let dot=va[0]*vb[0]+va[1]*vb[1]+va[2]*vb[2];
  dot=Math.max(-1,Math.min(1,dot));
  const ang=Math.acos(dot);
  if(ang<1e-8) return a.slice();
  const s=Math.sin(ang);
  const w1=Math.sin((1-u)*ang)/s, w2=Math.sin(u*ang)/s;
  return toLL([va[0]*w1+vb[0]*w2, va[1]*w1+vb[1]*w2, va[2]*w1+vb[2]*w2]);
}
```

```js
function slerpLL(a,b,u){
  const va=toV(a),vb=toV(b);
  let dot=va[0]*vb[0]+va[1]*vb[1]+va[2]*vb[2];
  dot=Math.max(-1,Math.min(1,dot));
  const ang=Math.acos(dot);
  if(ang<1e-8) return a.slice();
  const s=Math.sin(ang);
  const w1=Math.sin((1-u)*ang)/s, w2=Math.sin(u*ang)/s;
  return toLL([va[0]*w1+vb[0]*w2, va[1]*w1+vb[1]*w2, va[2]*w1+vb[2]*w2]);
}
```

```js
function acPos(ac,t){
  const L=ac.legs;
  if(t<=L[0].t0){...return start}
  for(let i=0;i<L.length;i++){const g=L[i];
    if(t<=g.t1){
      const u=g.t1>g.t0?(t-g.t0)/(g.t1-g.t0):1;
      let ll;
      if(g.hold){ const ang=u*Math.PI*6; const rr=0.25; ll=[g.a[0]+rr*Math.sin(ang)*0.3? ...]}
      else ll=slerpLL(g.a,g.b,ease?no,linear u);
      const alt=g.alt0+(g.alt1-g.alt0)*smooth(u);
      return {ll,alt,leg:g};
    }
  }
  return end pos
}
```

```js
function slerpLL(a,b,u){
  const va=toV(a),vb=toV(b);
  let dot=va[0]*vb[0]+va[1]*vb[1]+va[2]*vb[2];
  dot=Math.max(-1,Math.min(1,dot));
  const ang=Math.acos(dot);
  if(ang<1e-8) return a.slice();
  const s=Math.sin(ang);
  const w1=Math.sin((1-u)*ang)/s, w2=Math.sin(u*ang)/s;
  return toLL([va[0]*w1+vb[0]*w2, va[1]*w1+vb[1]*w2, va[2]*w1+vb[2]*w2]);
}
```

```js
function acPos(ac,t){
  const L=ac.legs;
  if(t<=L[0].t0){...return start}
  for(let i=0;i<L.length;i++){const g=L[i];
    if(t<=g.t1){
      const u=g.t1>g.t0?(t-g.t0)/(g.t1-g.t0):1;
      let ll;
      if(g.hold){ const ang=u*Math.PI*6; const rr=0.25; ll=[g.a[0]+rr*Math.sin(ang)*0.3? ...]}
      else ll=slerpLL(g.a,g.b,ease?no,linear u);
      const alt=g.alt0+(g.alt1-g.alt0)*smooth(u);
      return {ll,alt,leg:g};
    }
  }
  return end pos
}
```
